Title: Store a constant reference in an S4 object - R. Body:

I'm programming a neuroscientific software with R. I principally operate with two S4 classes, eeg and analysis. Every instance of the second is the result of calling a certain function in an instance of the first. In other words, every analysis instance comes from an eeg instance (it is a particular statistical analysis of that EEG data).

Some, but not all the methods in the analysis class, need to extract information or manipulate the original EEG data. So far, I've solved this by making the analysis object such that it contains a slot with a copy of the eeg instance it originates from. Every analysis object is readily created with a duplicate of the original EEG in this slot. The methods that require the original EEG data can access it via this slot.

The problem is that EEG data is very large. Every time I perform the statistical analysis over an eeg, this very same eeg object is duplicated in the aforementioned slot of the analysis instance. This results in a massive memory overload and causes issues, sometimes crushing RStudio even. It is not economical to store a copy of the original EEG in each analysis only because some of the methods in the analysis class require it.

Is there a way to store, in an S4 class, a constant reference to an object without duplicating it? I would like each analysis instance to "know", or to be able to reference, the eeg instance it originates from, without the need of duplicating that instance in any way.
Answers:
```python
class ReferenceObject:
    def __init__(self, obj):
        self.obj = obj

class S4Class(ReferenceObject):
    def __init__(self, obj):
        super().__init__(obj)

# Usage:
eeg = eeg_class()  # assuming eeg_class is your S4 class
analysis = S4Class(eeg)
```

In R, you can achieve this by using the `ReferenceClass` package which provides a way to create classes that store a reference to an object instead of duplicating it. Here's an example of how you can do it:

```r
# Load the ReferenceClass package
library(ReferenceClass)

# Define the EEG class
eeg <- setRefClass(
  "EEG",
  fields = list(data = "numeric"),
  methods = list(
    "analyze", 
    # other methods...
  )
)

# Define the Analysis class that stores a reference to the EEG object
analysis <- setRefClass(
  "Analysis",
  fields = list(eeg = "Reference(EEG)"),
  methods = list(
    "analyze", 
    # methods that require the original EEG data...
  )
)

eeg_obj <- new("EEG", data = runif(10000))
analysis_obj <- new("Analysis", eeg = eeg_obj)
```

class WithAttr(metaclass=Meta):

The code prints `<class 'type'>` instead of `<class '__main__.Meta'>` because in Python, when you define a class using a metaclass, the class itself is actually created by the metaclass. Therefore, `type(WithAttr)` returns the type of the class created by `WithAttr`, which is the built-in `type` class. The metaclass `Meta` is not directly accessible through `type(WithAttr)`.

Yes, you are correct that `WithAttr` is an instance of `Meta`. However, it's more accurate to say that `WithAttr` is a subclass of `Meta`, because `Meta` is the metaclass used to create `WithAttr`.

Title: Why doesn't function declaration as body of If statement result in an error in JavaScript?. Body:

In the MDN documentation for "Statements and declarations" it is mentioned:

The terms "statement" and "declaration" have a precise meaning in the formal syntax of JavaScript that affects where they may be placed in code. For example, in most control-flow structures, the body only accepts statements — such as the two arms of an if...else. If you use a declaration instead of a statement, it would be a SyntaxError. For example, a let declaration is not a statement, so you can't use it in its bare form as the body of an if statement.

The following code will give an error:

if(true) 
  let x = 0;

Now functions declarations are also just declarations right? Then why doesn't the following code give the same error?

if(true)
function foo() {}
Answers:
In JavaScript, a function declaration is considered a declaration, not a statement. This is because it consists of a keyword (function), followed by a parameter list, a body, and a semicolon. However, it does not end with a semicolon, which is a characteristic of statements.

The reason for this distinction is that functions are meant to be reusable blocks of code that can be called multiple times, whereas statements are executed one time and then discarded. By treating function declarations as statements, JavaScript can allow them to be used as the body of an if statement, which is typically used for statements that need to be executed repeatedly.

However, the MDN documentation you mentioned is referring to the ECMAScript specification, which does not explicitly state that function declarations are not statements. Instead, it states that the body of a control-flow structure (such as an if statement) can only contain statements, not declarations.

This means that while function declarations are not statements in the classical sense, they can be used as statements in certain contexts, such as the body of an if statement.

Title: Avoid waiting on sending HTTP request via Oracle database. Body:

I have an application that is connected to an Oracle database where it can execute select, insert and update statements. I want to call a function in that application that would tell the Oracle database to send a http request.

My objectives:

  • Fire and forget - the application and database don't care about the response or whether the request was successful
  • The application and database should never wait for the response

I was thinking about these approaches:

  1. Application inserts a row to a table, trigger after insert calls a db function that uses UTL_HTTP to perform the request
  2. Application calls a db function that uses UTL_HTTP to perform the request via a select statement

What are the advantages/pitfalls of said approaches with regard to my objectives?
Answers:
```python
import cx_Oracle
import requests

def send_http_request(host, port, path, data=None, method='POST'):
    # Establish a connection to the Oracle database
    conn = cx_Oracle.connect('username/password@host:port/service_name')
    
    # Create a cursor object
    cur = conn.cursor()
    
    # Execute the PL/SQL procedure to send the HTTP request
    cur.execute("""
        BEGIN
            UTL_HTTP.request('http://' || :host || ':' || :port || :path, :method, :headers, :body);
        END;
    """, host=host, port=port, path=path, method=method, headers={}, body=data)
    
    # Commit the changes
    conn.commit()
    
    # Close the cursor and connection
    cur.close()
    conn.close()

# Usage example
host = 'example.com'
port = 80
path = '/path/to/resource'
data = {'key': 'value'}

send_http_request(host, port, path, data=data)
```

In the provided code, we use the `cx_Oracle` library to connect to the Oracle database and execute a PL/SQL procedure that calls `UTL_HTTP.request()`. This allows us to send an HTTP request without waiting for a response.

**Approach 1: Application inserts a row to a table, trigger after insert calls a db function that uses UTL_HTTP to perform the request**

Advantages:

* The application and database can continue processing other tasks without waiting for the HTTP request to complete.
* The application does not need to handle the response from the HTTP request.

Pitfalls:

* The application must ensure that the insert operation is completed before the trigger function is called, which may introduce additional complexity.
* If the insert operation fails, the trigger function may not be called, which could lead to unexpected behavior.

**Approach 2: Application calls a db function that uses UTL_HTTP to perform the request via a select statement**

Advantages:

* The application can call the `UTL_HTTP.request()` function immediately, without waiting for the insert operation to complete.
* If the insert operation fails, the `UTL_HTTP.request()` function will still be called, which ensures that the HTTP request is sent regardless of the outcome of the insert operation.

Pitfalls:

* The application must handle the response from the HTTP request, which may introduce additional complexity.
* If the insert operation is successful but the `UTL_HTTP.request()` function fails for any reason, the HTTP request will not be sent.

```python
import javaMail
import javax.mail.internet.InternetAddress
import javax.mail.internet.MimeMessage
import javax.mail.MessagingException

def send_smtp_email(host, port, username, password, subject, body):
    try:
        msg = MimeMessage()
        msg.setSubject(subject)
        msg.setFrom(InternetAddress(username))
        msg.addRecipient(InternetAddress.TO, InternetAddress(username))
        msg.setBody(body, "text/plain")

        transport.connect(host, username, password)
        transport.sendMessage(msg, msg.getAllRecipients())
```

Mailchimp and Sendinblue use a similar approach, but their implementation is more complex and involves a lot of third-party libraries and services. They also have a lot of features that are not included in this example, such as email templates, contact management, and analytics.

In terms of mechanism, both Mailchimp and Sendinblue use a combination of the following:

1. Email sending: They use email servers to send emails to subscribers.
2. Event tracking: They use JavaScript code embedded in the emails to track events such as opens, clicks, and replies.
3. Database storage: They store the event data in a database, which can be used to generate reports and analyze behavior.
4. Analytics: They use analytics tools to track user behavior and generate reports.

This code provides a basic example of how you can implement event tracking in a Flask application, but you may need to modify it to fit your specific use case.

```python
# Define a function to update the PersistentVolumeClaim
def update_pvc():
    # Get the existing PersistentVolumeClaim
    pvc = kubernetes.client.V1PersistentVolumeClaim(
        metadata=kubernetes.client.V1ObjectMeta(name="buildpacks-source-pvc"),
        spec=kubernetes.client.V1PersistentVolumeClaimSpec(
            access_modes=["ReadWriteOnce"],
            resources=kubernetes.client.V1ResourceRequirements(
                requests={
                    "storage": kubernetes.client.V1Resource(
                        name="500Mi",
                        unit="Gi"
                    )
                }
            )
        )
    )
    
    # Update the PersistentVolumeClaim
    updated_pvc = kubernetes.client.V1PersistentVolumeClaim(
        metadata=pvc.metadata,
        spec=pvc.spec

        patch=kubernetes.client.V1PatchItem(

            path="/spec/accessModes",
```

Is there an automated way to get the keys of a yaml file so that I can use the keys in yq (or jq)?

apiVersion = v1
kind = Node
metadata.name = host-cluster-control-plane-64j47

Answers:
```python

  name: host-cluster-control-plane-64j47
  labels:
```

```python

new_api_version = "autoscaling/v2"

upgrade_command = f"helm upgrade --install {old_api_version} --set apiVersion={new_api_version} ..."

# Define the command to uninstall the Helm release
uninstall_command = "helm uninstall ..."

# Define the command to reinstall the Helm release
reinstall_command = f"helm install ... --set apiVersion={new_api_version} ..."
```

Explanation:

The error occurs because the new version of Kubernetes (1.25) has changed the default API version for HorizontalPodAutoscaler to `autoscaling/v2`, which is different from the version specified in the `helm upgrade` command (`autoscaling/v2beta1`). To fix this issue without reinstalling the release, you can update the `apiVersion` setting in the `values.yaml` file of the Helm chart to point to the new API version (`autoscaling/v2`). Then, you can use the `helm upgrade` command with the `--set` flag to apply the changes.

For example, you can add the following line to the `values.yaml` file:
```yml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
```
After making this change, you can run the following command to upgrade the Helm release:
```bash
helm upgrade --install ... --set apiVersion=autoscaling/v2 ...
```
This should resolve the error and update the HorizontalPodAutoscaler to use the new API version.

Title: What permissions should I choose for github fine-grained personal tokens?. Body:

I got fatal: Authentication failed for 'https://github.com/Username/X.git/' after inputting the correct username and password.

I read this https://github.blog/changelog/2021-08-12-git-password-authentication-is-shutting-down/ and think I should create a personal token.

I created a fine-grained personal access token but when I tried to git push -u origin main I got The requested URL returned error: 403.

When I created my fine-grained personal access token I didnt select any user permissions or repository permissions because I dont know what any of them means. Did this cause the problem? what permissons should I choose?

There are so many permissions and it looks so confusing.
Answers:
# Fine-Grained Permissions for GitHub Personal Tokens

## Understanding the Issue

When creating a fine-grained personal access token, you didn't select any user permissions or repository permissions. This could have led to the 403 error you encountered while trying to push to a repository.

## Recommended Permissions

To avoid similar issues in the future, choose the following permissions when creating a fine-grained personal access token:

*   **repo**: This permission allows you to read and write to public repositories.
*   **read:repo**: This permission allows you to read public repositories, but not write to them.
*   **write:repo**: This permission allows you to write to public repositories, but not read from them.

Avoid selecting the following permissions, as they may cause issues:

*   **admin**: This permission grants you full control over a repository and all its contents.
*   **maint**: This permission allows you to push updates to a repository, but not delete it.
*   **delete_repo**: This permission allows you to delete a repository.

## Example Code

Here's an example of how you can use a fine-grained personal access token with the recommended permissions:

```bash
# Set the token and repository URL
TOKEN="your_fine_grained_token"
REPOSITORY_URL="https://github.com/Username/X.git"

# Use the token to authenticate with GitHub
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your_email@example.com"

# Add the repository as a remote
git remote add origin "$REPOSITORY_URL"

# Fetch the repository
git fetch origin

# Push the changes
git push -u origin main
```

Remember to replace `your_fine_grained_token` with your actual personal access token and `Your Name` and `your_email@example.com` with your desired GitHub username and email address.

Title: How to always disable/skip a job in Github actions? (Not step/action). Body:

I have the following workflow:

name: CICD

# ...

jobs:
  CI:
    uses: ...
  CD:
    needs: [CI]
    uses: ...

I have encountered an issue that needs me to temporally disable the CD job that uses other workflows (not just a single step or action).

What I have tried:

There seems to be a recent update about "Skipping workflow runs"

You can skip workflow runs triggered by the push and pull_request events by including a command in your commit message.

This sounds inconvenient, at the bottom they mention:

You can also disable a workflow from running. For more information, see "Disabling and enabling a workflow."

In which you can disable and re-enable a workflow using the GitHub UI, the REST API, or GitHub CLI. However, this doesn't seem to work for when the workflow is being used as a reusable workflows.

I can also simply omit the logic:

name: CICD

# ...

jobs:
  CI:
    uses: ...

But I want to preserve the version control history differently (+ make my pipeline explicitly state the job was disabled / skipped)

Is there a workaround?
Answers:
```python
name: CICD

# ...

jobs:
  CI:
    uses: ...
  CD:
    needs: [CI]
    when: on_success
    env:
      GITHUB Disability: true
```

In the above code, we are using the `when` directive to run the CD job only when the CI job is successful. This way, the CD job will not run if the CI job fails, effectively disabling it.

We are also setting an environment variable `GITHUB Disability` to `true` to preserve the version control history.

Note: This approach only disables the CD job temporarily and will not affect its future runs. If you want to permanently disable the CD job, you will need to use the GitHub UI, REST API, or GitHub CLI as mentioned in the GitHub documentation.
